speaker: braddockhuesman
text: Thank you, Your Honors. Justice Carballito, Justice Torres, Justice Merriman, may it please the court. This appeal today is about whether Mr. Libby received a fair trial. He did not. And with my time today, I'd like to discuss the two reasons why he did not. First, Mr. Libby requested a new counsel. The trial court abused its discretion in denying that request, and in doing so, denied Mr. Libby the effective assistance of counsel. Second thing I'd like to talk about today is the fact that the trial judge's actions in this case, he crossed the line and gave the appearance of bias in this case. He supplied actual testimony, opinion testimony, and those actions crossed the line. Either of these two issues are sufficient for Mr. Libby to receive a new trial. With my time today, I'd like to discuss both. I'd like to first discuss the denial of effective assistance of counsel. The trial court failed to recognize a complete breakdown between Mr. Libby and his trial attorney. At the eve of trial, at right before voir dire, the trial counsel announced to the trial court that his client had a request to make. At that point, Mr. Libby made a pro se request to have his attorney removed and a new attorney appointed in his place. The judge immediately closed down the courtroom and conducted a new inquiry. Ultimately, the court denied that request, and in doing so, abused its discretion. To determine whether a trial court abuses its discretion in denying a pro se litigant's request for a new counsel, the court looks at three prong test. First, the adequacy of the court's inquiry. Second, the extent of the conflict between the attorney and the client. And third, the timeliness of the motion. I'll address each of those points today. The first prong is the inadequacy of the hearing the trial court judge conducted. Mr. Libby was a pro se litigant at this point when he asked for a new attorney. He is a defendant on trial against some serious charges. The trial court asked open-ended vague questions about why Mr. Libby wanted a new attorney. The trial court did not provide Mr. Libby the standards or exemplars that would indicate to a pro se litigant how to marshal his facts, how to meet the burden. This is a very real burden a litigant has to meet. And when you're dealing with a pro se litigant, I think we've cited these cases in our briefs, the judge has a heightened duty to make sure his rights to a fair trial and his rights to effective assistance counsel are protected. In this case, they were not. Because the trial court failed to provide those exemplars as suggested by the Castle case and some others that we've cited, the judge then compounded that error with general vague open-ended questions about why Mr. Libby wanted a new attorney. Tell me why you want a new attorney. How many times did you meet? What other reasons do you have for wanting a new attorney? Those might be fine if the judge has announced what the standard is, if the judge has announced exemplars of how to meet that. But you're dealing with a pro se litigant who doesn't necessarily understand how to marshal his facts and what facts he even needs to marshal, what might be important to a pro se litigant is not going to be the same thing to an attorney. That happens all the time. And so-

text: Good morning, Chief Justice. May it please the court. This is a case where a defendant has been convicted with overwhelming evidence against him. So the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is not absolute. It is qualified by certain compelling interests, such as avoidance of delay, and a defendant is not entitled to have a particular lawyer with whom he can have a meaningful relationship. That is actually what the law says. In other words, defendants have a right to be represented by counsel, competent counsel at trial, but they don't have a right to choose a particular counsel. If they don't like what that counsel is saying, they don't have a right to say, I want a different free second opinion. speaker: richellecanto
text: I think what happened there, Your Honor, is when the record is read, it appears defense counsel had asked several questions already that were very long, and at some points argumentative, and I think confusing to the jury. Now, I will concede that it touches on the point where it would become troubling because the court maybe said more things than he should have said. However, I think the intent and the effect was a clarification of the evidence. And 614 allows courts to do that. The law has said that statements by trial courts are deemed improper when they answer specific questions on behalf of witnesses with responses that were not even suggested by their testimony. But here, that's not the case. The witness had already said, no, there's a general order. No, I've never seen any other officer take out their phones and record. And I think when the judge stepped in here it was after several pages of the defense questioning the witness and having a hard time eliciting the evidence from this officer that he doesn't even own an iPhone and that he wouldn't take his Android phone out to record because it would get confiscated. And so I think what the court did was just try to help the presentation of evidence along, which is well within his authority. Do I think that he could have put it in a better, more prudent way? Yes. But do I think that this is improper or warrants a new trial? No. Our argument is that no substantial rights were prejudiced here because even if the entirety of Officer Escavo's testimony was about the recording, the arrest and the arrest was not there, there was still overwhelming evidence here and that he would have been found guilty. He was arrested at three in the morning. He was wearing a burglar outfit. He had stolen jewelry and tools in his pocket. The victim had observed him sneaking out of his house and ran after him to try to apprehend him in the middle of the road at 3 a.m. And there was a whole surveillance video of him stealing the items from inside the home. And so if there was any error here, assuming that the court erred, maybe overstepped and said a little bit more than he should have, it should be reviewed for plain error. And under that kind of analysis, the trial court's errors did not prejudice the defendant and the result would have been the same. He would have still been found guilty by a jury because of the overwhelming evidence. And to Mr. Hughesman's point, I actually don't think that this is a fundamental error or a structural error. The case that he cites is Toomey, for example, where the judge there was a mayor who could have only been paid for his services as a judge if he convicted those that were brought before him. That's not the case here. And here we're dealing with more of stray statements that were made by the judge that doesn't amount to a structural defect. The standard here is whether or not the error was plain because he didn't object to trial and the government maintains this is not, there is no substantial right that was prejudiced here. The court has a duty also to consider the trial record as a whole and ignore errors that are harmless, including most constitutional violations. There was no error when the court denied his request for a new counsel and participated at trial. And if any error was made, it did not affect his substantial rights. So in conclusion, justices, the people asked the court to affirm the defendant's conviction here.
